page: Google Cloud Platform n4-highcpu-2 is an x86_64 architecture server belonging to the n4 family. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from a single physical Intel core with hyper-threading enabled, resulting in 2 threads per core. The instance is equipped with 4.0 GB of system memory, providing a resource density of 2.0 GB of RAM per core. It does not include any bundled local storage, GPU accelerators, or complimentary public IPv4 addresses. The processor features a cache hierarchy consisting of 48 KB L1d, 2 MB L2, and 260 MB L3 cache, alongside support for advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions.

Benchmark data reveals a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core capabilities. The server achieves average performance in single-core metrics, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1657.98 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1836.0. However, multi-core and memory-bound operations show significant limitations. The stress-ng multi-core performance is rated poor at 1736.79, and the Geekbench multi-core score is weak at 2242.0. Memory bandwidth is a notable bottleneck, with large-block read and write speeds falling into the poor category at 17.81 GB/sec and 11.0 GB/sec respectively.

Due to its low memory-to-CPU ratio and constrained memory bandwidth, this server is poorly suited for memory-intensive applications, database operations, or complex multi-threaded tasks. Passmark database operations scored poorly at 1006.28, and Redis SET operations reached only 2.31 million operations per second. However, the inclusion of AVX-512 and AMX instruction sets provides hardware-level acceleration for specific vector and matrix operations. The instance is best utilized for lightweight, single-threaded compute tasks, basic text processing, or entry-level web serving where high memory capacity and high multi-core throughput are not required.

Benchmarks indicate average single-core performance, with a Geekbench single-core score of 1836.0, but weak to poor multi-core and memory bandwidth results, such as a large-block read speed of 17.81 GB/sec. Consequently, database operations and memory-heavy tasks perform poorly.
